title: An Exploration of Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent: Muon and its Many Variants
claim: Baseline optimizers need precise learning-rate tuning, while our variants reach low loss across a much wider range of rates.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots; left LR sweep, right training curves
description: Two line plots sit side by side. The left plot shows final validation loss against Muon learning rate on a log x-axis from 1e-4 to 1e1, with a y-range of about 3.1 to 4.0. The gray Scion line and the solid blue MuonAdam line form sharp, narrow V shapes that shoot off the top of the plot away from a minimum near 1e-2. The dotted blue MuonAdam-Momo line and the dotted pink MuonMax-Momo line stay flat and low, near 3.15 to 3.2, over several orders of magnitude. The right plot shows noisy training loss against epochs from 0.60 to 1.00. Scion is highest, and the other three curves sit close together lower down, with pink lowest. A legend in each plot uses the same color coding. The eye goes first to the sharp V curves on the left. The crop also includes the date line and the abstract text above the plots.
caption: Learning rate sweep for training GPT2-Large (774M params) on SlimPajama with 1B tokens. Left: Final validation loss for various learning rates. \alg{MuonAdam} and \alg{Scion} require precise tuning, whereas our \alg{MuonAdam}-\alg{Momo} and \alg{MuonMax}-\alg{Momo} achieve low loss for a significantly wider range of learning rates. Right: Training loss (with tuned LRs) for the last 40% of steps.
abstract: To define a steepest descent method over a neural network, we need to choose a norm for each layer, a way to aggregate these norms across layers, and whether to use normalization. We systematically explore different alternatives for aggregating norms across layers, both formalizing existing combinations of Adam and the recently proposed Muon as a type of non-Euclidean gradient descent, and deriving new variants of the Muon optimizer. Through a comprehensive experimental evaluation of the optimizers within our framework, we find that Muon is sensitive to the choice of learning rate, whereas a new variant we call MuonMax is significantly more robust. We then show how to combine any non-Euclidean gradient method with model based momentum (known as Momo). The new Momo variants of Muon are significantly more robust to hyperparameter tuning, and often achieve a better validation score. Thus for new tasks, where the optimal hyperparameters are not known, we advocate for using Momo in combination with MuonMax to save on costly hyperparameter tuning.
